Briefing: Clumsy parking can quickly make a set of handsome alloy wheels look ugly, but so can brake dust. Car brakes rely on friction between the pads and rotor to provide a deceleration force, so every time you press the brake pedal, both shed tiny fragments.

Clumsy parking can quickly make a set of handsome alloy wheels look ugly, but so can brake dust. Car brakes rely on friction between the pads and rotor to provide a deceleration force, so every time you press the brake pedal, both shed tiny fragments. Some are carried away by the air and are more harmful to our lungs than diesel emissions , one study found. But others settle on your shiny wheels, creating a dull coating that can make even the tidiest low-mileage car look like a haggard workhorse. And it's not just track-day cars that suffer from a buildup of dust. Yes, hitting the brakes hard will release more dust, and spoil wheels faster, but even the kind of gentle braking used in daily driving can quickly coat your rims.

Washing your car and wheels regularly is the best way to keep the brake dust away, though it's easy for that routine to slip when you're busy. But there's a good reason why you ought to make the effort. Because the longer you leave it on the wheels, the harder it is to get rid of with simple cleaning materials. And dust can even cause permanent staining if really neglected. If that happens, you could be looking at a bill of around $150 per wheel to have them professionally repaired.

The original Avanti was not only one of the coolest cars of its era, but it also once held the record for fastest production car on the market. The Avanti was famous for delivering serious world-beating performance to the American market years before the Big Three went hog wild in the heady muscle car days of the late 1960s.

With company president Sherwood Egbert taking the reins in 1961 and eager to make an impression, he gave Loewy just six weeks to design the now-iconic high-performance halo car for the brand. Egbert's philosophical demand for the Avanti was that it "must be tops in speed, braking, handling, safety features, and general innovation—and please don't spend any money." Costco is much more than just a go-to place to buy groceries cheaply and in bulk. The retailer sells hardware, electronics, cleaning supplies, and appliances. Costco can also be an excellent place to buy tires at discounted prices. But are tires from Costco the same quality as those sold at more traditional outlets? Yes, they're exactly the same.

A key reason why tires are often so cheap at Costco is buying power. The retail giant negotiates directly with manufacturers and places large orders, allowing it to secure discounts and then sell tires more cheaply to its members. Costco also sells a more limited range of tires than many dedicated wheel and tire stores. By limiting choice, it can secure even better deals with its suppliers. Costco also operates narrow margins on its tires as it makes up to 70% of its operating profit from membership fees.

And in that case, it's probably also true that you're hardly itching to shell out for a massive weekly thrashing at the pump. After all, however you define a classic, they tend to be parts-and-labor-costs hungry. At the time of this writing, AAA says the national average for a gallon of gas sits at $4.12, up 36% versus a year ago, when it was $3.04. And in California a gallon of regular will run you $5.87. Ouch.

Plus you've got a pocket humblebrag at the ready wherever you cruise in your fuel-sipping steed. Imagine showing up at a cars and coffee with your vintage ride and telling the assembled dudes (always, always, dudes) that your 1990 Honda CRX gets a combined 40-ish mpg – which torches the fuel economy of most modern cars.

Freeways are to people what arteries are to red blood cells. Most freeways consist of three or four lanes of synchronized traffic flow (or collective halt), but have you ever wondered what the world record is for the highest number of lanes on a freeway? The obvious choice would be the Katy Freeway on I-10 just west of Houston, which has no fewer than 26 traffic lanes spread across both directions at its widest. However, that number also includes feeder roads that don't actually form part of the I-10, so it's often argued that the "true" number is actually 18.

If that's the case, a few other massive highways may indeed lay claim to Katy's title as the highest-lane highway in the world. Canada, for instance, has an 18-lane road approaching one of its airports, while Burma's capital city has a section with up to 20 lanes. However, perhaps the biggest threats sit halfway across the globe in China. These include a special section of the G4 Beijing–Hong Kong-Macau Expressway and the Hefei–Nanjing Expressway, the latter of which can open up to as many as 36 separate lanes — but with one very important caveat. Let's take a look at some of the highest-lane freeways in the world and how they compare before crowning the winner.

item.content:encoded:
Briefing: Mention a Chevy Impala, and thoughts of an unremarkable family sedan may come to mind, but add an SS next to the nameplate and things change. Mention a Chevy Impala, and thoughts of an unremarkable family sedan may come to mind, but add an SS next to the nameplate and things change. The Impala SS (Super Sport) is a pure horsepower play that dates back to 1961, two years after the Bowtie brand launched the Impala as a standalone model. Its numbers are still impressive, even by 21st-century standards. The retail version of the Impala SS from the 1960s, which covered two generations, produced up to 425 horsepower. The later Impala SS generations from the 1990s and 2000s were less brutish, offering between 240 and 303 hp, but they were still a step up from their more mundane counterparts.

However, these horsepower numbers come with a catch. The output figures for 1960s Impala SS models reflected gross horsepower ratings, which generally didn't account for intake, exhaust, and accessory loads. When the 1970s rolled around, the auto industry was dealing with tighter emissions regulations and insurance companies that took a dim view of high-powered cars. By the 1972 model year, Detroit switched to net horsepower calculations to better reflect real-world engine configurations. Because gross horsepower ratings often varied from manufacturer to manufacturer, there's no standard way to convert horsepower ratings between the methods, but both still measure horsepower at the crankshaft, not the wheels.

Technically, directional tires can be rotated from one side of a car to the other. Nobody can stop you from unbolting a wheel/tire combo from one side of the car and putting it on the other side. The catch is that doing it properly involves more work than unbolting the wheels and swapping their positions. Skip that extra work and those carefully designed tread patterns will end up running backward. That might not sound all that terrible, but for these "unidirectional" tires, the rolling direction matters.

Crossing directional tires requires removing them from their wheels and remounting them in the correct orientation for the opposite side. Each one then needs rebalancing, which is where the red and yellow dots on tires come in. So sure, you can unbolt whatever is on the passenger side of your car and swap it to the driver's side. But the tread will be heading in the wrong direction. Still, there are other ways to do this job without messing anything up.

The Hummer brand officially launched in 1992 with the debut of its AM General High Mobility Multipurpose Wheeled Vehicle military-based civilian model. Much like the popularity of the Willys Jeep in post-WWII America, the H1 capitalized on rah-rah post-Gulf War nationalism and a personal endorsement from Arnold Schwarzenegger to find its place in the automotive zeitgeist. After being awarded its first military production contract in 1983, the big diesel-powered machine was well-proven by the time John Q. Public could place an order a decade later. If the HMMWV can be relied on by our fighting finest in the Muthanna Province, then surely it'll withstand the rigors of your suburban commute, right? Well, as it turns out, the answer is a cryptically Schrödinger-esque yes and no.

When it comes to imposing four-wheeled machines, there's nothing quite as eye-catching and road-commanding as the original Hummer. Between 1992 and 1999, the vehicle was sold in small quantities by AM General's civilian division, but General Motors purchased the rights to market and distribute the Hummer brand for the new millennium. With just shy of 12,000 units sold across the truck's entire production run, these things are a bit thin on the ground, but they maintain a strong cultural significance today, and the appeal of a genuine mil-spec vehicle is hard to deny.

The Elon Musk venture SpaceX, for example, is building new natural gas pipelines in order to produce its own methane-based propellant, needed to sustain the launch of many thousands of rockets in the coming years.

Not all rocket fuel is methane-based, but that’s where some aerospace firms, including SpaceX, have landed in the pursuit of space domination. Methane is processed from natural gas, stripping away nitrogen and other impurities. Liquefied and mixed with liquid oxygen, it becomes a powerful propellant.

Tom Gage is the one-time CEO of a company you probably don't remember, called AC Propulsion. However, that firm was one of the progenitors of EVs and, by extension, Tesla. Gage is also the one-time owner of this 1994 Honda Civic. This past weekend he sold it, and we should explain why that's important.

See, underneath its aged sheet metal, it wasn't a Civic at all, but more of a science experiment. It has no tailpipe because Gage's partner, AC Propulsion co-founder Alan Cocconi, gutted the little hatchback in 1994 to fill with lead-acid bricks and convert the Civic into a proof-of-concept electric car that led to the rise of Tesla. The Tesla link is that AC Propulsion used the Civic to try out systems that would later debut on the company's 1998 tzero electric Roadster. That car looked cooler, but had the same tech that powered the electric Honda. And it's that technology that Tesla eventually licensed in 2004 and that ended up featuring in the original Tesla Roadster in 2008.

Stories about Flock cameras and other stalkerish automatic license plate readers (ALPRs) have been a mainstay of American news for the last year or two, and horror stories involving this questionable technology are everywhere. From police using ALPRs to stalk citizens to AI-powered ALPRs flagging innocent auto journalists for stealing vehicles , there's no shortage of evidence that ALPRs are making the world worse. A lot of such stories you see in the news and even here on Jalopnik are about misuse of and issues with ALPRs specifically in the United States, though. While there's certainly some bias toward American news on publications based in the States, it still does raise the question: Are there Flock cameras or equivalents in other countries? And if so, do they cause the same volume of issues?

The answer is an interesting one. First, yes, ALPRs do exist outside of the United States, though the technology is often called automatic number plate recognition, or ANPR, due to regional differences in how license plates are referred to. Nearly 100 countries use this technology to track automobile movement and other data. However, Flock cameras themselves aren't nearly as prevalent outside the United States. In fact, the big difference between the implementation of license plate recognition technology in the U.S. and abroad is in who owns it and how the data collected is managed.

The future of American access to space is in doubt for the first time in decades. That very uncertainty is already starting to show itself as an opportunity for the companies positioned to seize it. In the last few weeks, the Pentagon has handed out two separate $150 million loans to rocket companies Stoke Space and Rocket Lab, investments meant to build out their launch infrastructure and manufacturing capabilities. That ought to help get them to a place where they can reliably launch military assets into space, but critically, it also helps them attract and deliver on commercial contracts, too. Business is booming, and a lot more is expected to come the way of these two and many other rocket companies in the next few years. The main reason: SpaceX, the dominant force in the entire sector, is giving that business away.

Elon Musk's rocket enterprise has expanded a lot lately, getting into everything from AI infrastructure to natural gas mining . Its future mainly depends on the in-development Starship rocket, however. The largest and most powerful rocket ever built, it is supposedly taking astronauts to the Moon and is the only rocket that can deploy Starlink's newest V3 satellites. SpaceX really, really needs Starship to work. So it's acting as if it will work, which means the company has already stopped taking reservations for flights on its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket . While it appears that the military and NASA may get a few extra years to use that rocket , Musk has made it clear he intends to wind down the Falcon 9 sooner rather than later.

The current 250-series Land Cruiser sold in the U.S. is based on the smaller Prado model sold in other countries. It is not only physically smaller than the 200-series it replaced, but it also has a much lower price tag as well. In 2021, the 200-series Land Cruiser started at a little more than $87,000 with delivery, processing, and handling fees. Today, a new Land Cruiser 1958 starts at $59,775, all fees included. That is a significant price cut for what is still a very capable body-on-frame SUV.

It lived through the Malaise era, took on competition from all manner of American rivals, and even went on to find considerable success in other markets – no easy feat for a muscle car. Through those years, we've been blessed with a total of seven Mustang generations, but we shouldn't pretend each one was as brilliant as the next. While the first-gen model has gone down as an important slice of American motoring history, the Mustang II that followed is largely best left forgotten. However, the third generation, known as the Fox Body Mustang, rescued the Mustang's reputation as a muscle car and stood the test of time.

These cars debuted as '79 model years, and were not replaced until the SN95 cars marched onto the scene for 1994. Throughout those years, an estimated 2.6 million Fox Body Mustangs found owners, making it by far one of the most successful Mustang generations. Among them, though, were some exceedingly rare variants, such as the immensely sought-after 1-of-107 SVT Cobra R, and the 3,003 Feature Cars of '93, and the 1985 Twister II Mustang.

Like it or not, turbocharged engines are becoming more common. In fact, of the 16.3 million new passenger vehicles sold in the U.S. in 2025, 45% of them were equipped with a turbocharged engine. Automakers are squeezing every drop out power out of smaller engines while trying to reduce fuel consumption, and adding a turbocharger is how many choose to do it. There are trade-offs for these performance perks, though. The most notorious is that there will be some turbo lag, unless you run a supercharger and a turbocharger at once . One trade-off that is mentioned less frequently, though, is that compared to naturally aspirated engines, turbocharged engines require specially formulated oil that needs to be changed more often.
